extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, peer reviewers, research integrity officers, and researchers interested in publication ethics
extracted.subtask_short: detecting fake peer review and paper mills
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for detecting and preventing fake peer review (FPR), paper-mill manuscripts, and related misconduct, aimed at improving editorial procedures and research integrity. Covers indicators of fraud, editorial and publisher countermeasures, and policy/educational recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of Fake Peer Review (FPR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clues that a suggested or supplied reviewer is fake or manipulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for generic e-mail addresses provided by potential reviewers who are difficult to find online; review accounts delivered within a few days or even hours; and reviews worded quite favorably. Authors may abuse automated submission systems to suggest reviewers and supply e-mail addresses created by the submitters themselves who then fabricate favorable reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove author-suggested reviewer option
rubrics_metrics.description: Preventing authors from suggesting reviewers via submission systems to reduce opportunity for FPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some publishers have removed the option for authors to suggest reviewers from their online submission systems as a measure to avoid fake peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify reviewer identity (names and e-mails)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must verify the name and email address of every potential peer reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify especially when a famous scientist is presented with a noninstitutional or generic account; confirm institutional affiliation and online presence to ensure the reviewer is genuine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use universal researcher identifiers and reviewer records
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt ORCID and check reviewer contributions on platforms like Publons to identify genuine reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop strategies to identify genuine reviewers (e.g., via ORCID) or by looking at reviewers' records in Publons to reduce reliance on email-only identity cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check conflicts of interest between referees and authors/editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure referees have no relevant conflicts of interest with submitting authors or editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should check for lack of any relevant conflict of interest before assigning reviewers, as undisclosed relationships can indicate manipulation or bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain peer review records long-term
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain peer review records to enable later investigation of manipulation or inappropriate behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CLUE recommendation: retain peer review records for at least 10 years to enable investigation of peer review manipulation or other inappropriate behaviour by authors or reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal risk factors for FPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of journals that correlate with higher rates of FPR-related retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FPR-related retractions often occur in journals with low (<5 or <2) or null Clarivate impact factor, many OA journals (including some OA mega journals), and journals that are domestic/non-indexed. Use these risk signals to apply heightened scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting paper-mill signs: recycled/duplicated figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper-mill manuscripts often reuse or recycle figures across unrelated submissions and journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for recycled figures widely spread among unrelated clients; detecting inter-journal duplication may require specialized image-manipulation or forensic software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting paper-mill signs: fake peer recommendations and industrialized production
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper mills may include fake peer recommendations and produce manuscripts in an industrialized, template-driven way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert for standardized text, implausible authorship patterns, fake reviewer recommendations, and rapid multiple submissions that suggest brokered or on-demand production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify reagents, methods, and experimental details
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and reviewers should verify reported reagents and details of how they were used in submitted research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request clear reagent identification and usage details; inconsistencies or vague reporting can indicate fabricated or low-quality research commonly associated with paper mills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request and scrutinize raw data before acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Require authors to provide raw data and scrutinize it carefully as part of acceptance checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and reviewers should request raw datasets and examine them for plausibility, manipulation, or duplication prior to accepting a manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use image-forensics tools to detect manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply specialized image manipulation/software tools to detect duplicated or manipulated images across submissions and journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because recycled or manipulated figures can be spread widely, use automated and manual image-forensic checks during review and editorial checks to spot inter-journal duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-submission transparency (preprint/receipt posting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place submitted papers and receipt dates in the public domain to deter deceptive simultaneous submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals could post submitted papers and the receipt date in a preprint server to place them publicly and thus avoid deceptive manuscripts and simultaneous multiple-journal submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen post-publication review and corrective notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve post-publication processes and use neutral editorial notices to report verifiable errors distinctly from expressions of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should provide editorial notices (distinct from expressions of concern) that neutrally describe reported and verifiable errors; enhance post-publication review to correct the literature effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise institutional and publisher policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Update and strengthen institutional and publisher policies to address fake papers, authors, e-mails, affiliations, and paper-mill phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions and publishers should revise policies, improve investigation procedures, and increase collaboration between research institutions and journals (e.g., CLUE recommendations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Education, training, and shared responsibility in research ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Strengthen education and awareness programs and foster shared responsibility among team members for research integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Countries and institutions (especially where researchers are financially rewarded for publications) should implement training in research ethics and awareness-raising programs for students, researchers, and other agents; promote shared responsibility across the research team to reduce pathogenic division of labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destigmatize retractions and use corrective (not punitive) approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat retractions as corrective measures rather than purely punitive to encourage error reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational programs should destigmatize withdrawals so that reporting errors is not combative or corrosive; encourage neutral, corrective communication to improve scientific self-correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address perverse incentives (monetary and metric-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and correct reward schemes (cash bonuses, metric-driven incentives) that incentivize poor publishing behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abolish or reform systems that pay cash bonuses per paper or reward quantity over quality; consider adjusting journal- and author-based metrics (e.g., IF) to account for retractions and undeserved citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must not rely solely on automated systems; use editorial intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated online submission/processing systems cannot substitute for editorial judgement and intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even the best online systems cannot replace editorial scrutiny; editors should apply professional judgement to detect anomalies that automated checks miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate with research institutions and investigative bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Strengthen cooperation between journals and institutions to investigate suspected misconduct and fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow CLUE-type recommendations to improve liaison between universities and editors, share evidence, and conduct thorough institutional investigations when manipulation is suspected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply heightened scrutiny to submissions from identified hotspots or patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize geographic, institutional, or authorship patterns associated with elevated retraction or misconduct rates and apply additional checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies show higher retraction rates or FPR prevalence in certain countries, journals, and institutions; such signals should prompt targeted integrity checks (without stigmatizing legitimate researchers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust bibliometric credit for journals and authors affected by fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct metrics (e.g., impact factor, citation credit) to account for undue benefit derived from fraudulent publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider corrective factors for author- and journal-based metrics impacted by citations from fraudulent or retracted work, to avoid rewarding misconduct.
